Raymond III Count of Tripoli was a nobleman who ruled the County of Tripoli in the 12th century 
He was born around 1142 and died in 1183 
His father was Raymond II Count of Tripoli and his mother was Melisende of Jerusalem 
Raymond III was a member of the House of Saint-Germain

* **Early Life and Succession** 
Raymond III became the Count of Tripoli after the death of his father Raymond II in 1163 
He was still a minor when he inherited the title and the county was governed by regents until he reached adulthood 
Raymond III took control of the county around 1170 

Raymond III played an important role in the politics of the Kingdom of Jerusalem 
He was a cousin of King Amalric I of Jerusalem and often advised him on military matters 
Raymond III participated in several battles against the Fatimid Caliphate and the Ayyubid dynasty 
He was known for his military skills and his knowledge of the region 

* **Marriage and Alliances** 
Raymond III married Isabella of Antioch but the marriage was childless 
He formed alliances with other Christian states in the region including the Principality of Antioch 
Raymond III also interacted with Muslim leaders and formed temporary alliances when necessary 

Raymond III died in 1183 without an heir 
The County of Tripoli passed to his cousin Bohemond III of Antioch 
Raymond III's death led to a period of instability in the region 

* **Legacy and Military Campaigns** 
Raymond III is remembered for his military campaigns and his role in the politics of the Kingdom of Jerusalem 
He was a skilled leader who fought against the forces of Saladin 
Raymond III's legacy has been studied by historians who have analyzed his impact on the region 
His military strategies and alliances have been the subject of historical research 

Raymond III Count of Tripoli was an important figure in the history of the Crusades 
He ruled the County of Tripoli during a time of conflict and uncertainty 
Raymond III's life and reign are well documented in historical sources 
He remains a significant character in the study of medieval history and the Crusades
